section.title: Node.js vs Python — Server-Side Concepts
section.subtitle: Runtime, packages, async programming, modules, files, HTTP servers, JSON and errors.

topics.title: Runtime & Execution Model
topics.learn: How each runtime executes your code.

node.definition: Node.js runs JavaScript on the V8 engine (same as Chrome). It is single-threaded with an event loop — ideal for I/O-heavy apps like APIs and real-time servers.

python.definition: Python code is interpreted line-by-line by the CPython interpreter. The GIL allows only one thread to run Python bytecode at a time, so concurrency relies on asyncio or multi-processing.
python.code:
# python app.py — interpreted, no compilation step
import sys
print('Hello from Python', sys.version)

# For concurrency use asyncio or multiprocessing.

node.definition: npm (bundled with Node) installs packages from the npm registry into node_modules. package.json declares dependencies; package-lock.json pins exact versions.

python.definition: pip installs packages from PyPI into site-packages. requirements.txt (or pyproject.toml) declares dependencies and pinned versions.
python.code:
pip install flask

# requirements.txt
Flask==3.0.0

# use it
from flask import Flask
app = Flask(__name__)

node.definition: Node is natively asynchronous — I/O uses callbacks, Promises and async/await. The event loop juggles thousands of connections in one thread.

python.definition: Python offers threads (limited by the GIL), multiprocessing, and asyncio with async/await for I/O-bound concurrency.
python.code:
import asyncio

async def get_user(uid):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return {'id': uid}

async def main():
    user = await get_user(1)
    print(user)

asyncio.run(main())

node.definition: CommonJS uses require() to import and module.exports to export. Modern code also supports ES modules with import/export (type: "module" in package.json).

python.definition: Python imports modules with the import statement. Each .py file is a module; __init__.py marks a package. Imports can pull specific names with from x import y.
python.code:
# math_utils.py
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

# app.py
from math_utils import add
print(add(2, 3))  # 5

node.definition: The built-in fs module reads/writes files asynchronously (non-blocking) or synchronously with *Sync variants.

python.definition: Built-in open() reads/writes files using a context manager (with) that auto-closes the file. pathlib offers an object-oriented API.
python.code:
# read + write with context manager
with open('data.txt', 'r') as f:
    text = f.read()

with open('out.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write(text.upper())

# pathlib style
from pathlib import Path
Path('out2.txt').write_text(text)

topics.title: HTTP Server
topics.learn: Creating a basic web server / API.

node.definition: Node's built-in http module (or Express on top) creates servers. Everything is a request/response cycle handled by callbacks — no extra runtime needed.

python.definition: Python's http.server handles basic serving; frameworks like Flask or FastAPI provide routing and JSON APIs on top of the standard library.

topics.title: JSON Handling
topics.learn: Parsing and producing JSON — the lingua franca of APIs.

node.definition: JSON is built into JavaScript: JSON.parse() converts text to objects, JSON.stringify() converts objects to text.

python.definition: The json module converts between Python dicts/lists and JSON strings with json.loads() and json.dumps().
python.code:
import json

text = '{"name": "Alice", "age": 30}'
obj = json.loads(text)
print(obj['name'])  # Alice

out = json.dumps({'ok': True, 'count': 2})
print(out)  # {"ok": true, "count": 2}

node.definition: JavaScript uses try/catch/finally. You can throw any value, but Error objects carry stack traces. Async errors surface as rejected Promises.

python.definition: Python uses try/except/else/finally. Built-in exception classes (ValueError, TypeError…) are raised with raise and caught by type.
